newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Protesters maintain pressure on Albanian leaders.
newsitem.headline: Protesters maintain pressure on Albanian leaders.

text.p: Protesters staged a ninth day of anti-government demonstrations in this troubled Adriatic port town on Thursday, hours after a policeman was shot dead in what authorities described as a brutal gangland killing.

Prosecutors said the shooting was unrelated to this week's clashes in Vlore, scene of some of the worst unrest Albania has seen since communism was toppled in 1990. One man was shot dead and two others died of heart attacks during pitched battles between protesters and police.
"First indications suggest this was a personal settling of accounts linked to a previous murder," investigating prosecutor Ramazan Ilica told Reuters.

The policeman, identified as Shezai Zani, 30, was killed by automatic gunfire on Wednesday near his home in a Vlore suburb, an Interior Ministry statement said. Ilica said 13 spent cartridges had been found near his body.
Local police said Zani was in charge of guarding "places of special importance" and had not played a role in the clashes.
Some 3,000 protesters resumed their daily routine of converging on Vlore's dilapidated central square, shouting "Down with the government" and "Resign, resign".

Albania has been rocked by anti-government protests and clashes over the past month after a series of dubious get-rich-quick investment schemes collapsed, robbing hundreds of thousands of their life savings in Europe's poorhouse.

Irate investors accuse the President Sali Berisha and the right-wing government of letting the funds flourish. Opposition parties said his Democratic Party used money from the schemes to finance a winning election campaign last year.

The government has denied the allegations. In an effort to contain the damage, it froze some $300 million deposited by two of the collapsed funds in local banks and has started paying some investors partial refunds.

Art students in Tirana, capital of the Balkan country of 3.4 million people, said they would stage a march later on Thursday, putting on colourful costumes and carrying signs appealing for non-violence.
Riot police have moved swiftly in Tirana in recent days to prevent any signs of protest.

On Wednesday, thousands of angry investors massing in Vlore, where Albania declared independence from Ottoman Turkish rule in 1912, cheered opposition leaders who have teamed up with trade unions to form a broad political alliance to try to topple the government.
"The government should resign because it is responsible for the biggest-ever theft from the Albanian people," the group said in a declaration.
The Vlore protests were sparked by the collapse of a local pyramid scheme in which most of the population had sunk their meagre life savings, leaving them penniless.

International criticism of the government's handling of the crisis intensified on Wednesday with the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe saying it was deeply worried about the violence. Britain expressed concern about reports of arrests and intimidation of opposition leaders.

Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi, in an interview with Italian daily Corriere della Sera, said the situation in Albania was under control "for the moment" and denied the demonstrator killed in Vlore had been shot by police.
